\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\bfig{79.8}{SII08_p2_phy_s2_q05_1.png}

\opt{C}{If $r_B=2$, then the total charge of the configuration is $15\pi k$.}

\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SII08-P2-PHY-S2-Q08, source={Score-II - Test 08 (05 Feb 2023)}, paper=2, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Electric field}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=8, diff_parts={K3 S1 I2 C2 F1}, diff_note={concepts: standard problem in this chapter, electric field, apply the relevant results | steps: apply the relevant results; compute}]
A disk of radius $R$ with uniform positive charge density $\sigma$ is placed on the $xy$ plane with its center at the origin. The Coulomb potential along the $z$-axis is $V(z) = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{R^2+z^2}-z\right)$. A particle of positive charge $q$ is placed initially at rest at a point on the $z$ axis with $z=z_0$ and $z_0>0$. In addition to the Coulomb force, the particle experiences a vertical force $\vec F = -c\hat k$ with $c>0$. Let $\beta=\dfrac{2c\epsilon_0}{q\sigma}$. Which of the following statement(s) is(are) correct?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{For $\beta=\dfrac14$ and $z_0=\dfrac{25}{7}R$, the particle reaches the origin.}
\opt{B}{For $\beta=\dfrac14$ and $z_0=\dfrac37R$, the particle reaches the origin.}
\opt{C}{For $\beta=\dfrac14$ and $z_0=\dfrac{R}{\sqrt3}$, the particle returns back to $z=z_0$.}
\opt{D}{For $\beta>1$ and $z_0>0$, the particle always reaches the origin.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

The center of cavity 'C' is the origin of a cartesian co-ordinate system shown. Points A, B and D are on the cavity surface on the axes. \opt{A}{For $\eta\to 0$, the electric field in the cavity is $\dfrac{\rho R}{3\varepsilon_0}$.}

\opt{C}{The same charge particle mentioned in option (B) is projected from point A towards C with speed $v_1$ for $\eta=\dfrac12$ so that it hits the surface of cavity at a point on x-axis. The speed must be $v_1=\dfrac{R}{2}\sqrt{\dfrac{\rho q}{6m\varepsilon_0}}$.}
\opt{D}{The change in kinetic energy of the charge particle mentioned in option (C) during it's motion before it collides is $\dfrac{\rho q R^2}{6\varepsilon_0}$.}
\end{qoptions}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA22-P2-PHY-S3-G17-18, source={Score Advanced - Test 22 (10 Apr 2024)}, questions={17-18}]
Consider first a metal sphere of radius R and total charge Q, which (because of symmetry) is distributed uniformly on its surface, i.e. the surface charge density is $\sigma_0=\dfrac{Q}{4\pi R^2}$ = constant.\par
The total field effects of the charges on the small surface pieces opposite each other cancel out in pairs, so the net electric field of all the charges on the sphere is zero at any point P inside the sphere. The same is shown in figure-1.\par
\bfig{92.7}{SA22_p2_phy_s3_para17_18_1.png}
\bfig{93.4}{SA22_p2_phy_s3_para17_18_2.png}
Now let us move on to the case of the electrically charged metal disc. We show that its charge distribution can be found from the uniform surface density of the charged metal sphere. Let us (notionally) `glue into position' the charges on the surface of the sphere, and then project the points of the spherical surface perpendicularly onto a plane that contains the centre of the sphere and point P investigated earlier.\par
As the charges cannot move, the charge $\Delta Q_1$, originally on the surface area $\Delta A_1$, when projected onto the plane, occupies a somewhat smaller area $\Delta A_1^{*}$, and so the surface charge density (with an unchanged amount of charge) increases. In addition, its distance from the point P also changes, from the original value of $r_1$ to the smaller one of $d_1$. The corresponding thing happens with the charge $\Delta Q_2$ originally located on the opposite side of the sphere.
\end{bankpassage}

\end{qoptions}

The field direction is perpendicular to the plane of plate. For this situation, mark out the correct statement (s). [In the options only big faces have been considered]:\par

\opt{D}{The electric field intensity at the surface of plate is discontinuous while potential is continuous.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=INT02-P1-PHY-S3-Q15, source={Internal Test - Test 02 (07 Jul 2021)}, paper=1, qno=15, type=numerical, subtopic={Electric potential}, answer={-19.2}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: potential energy of the hydrogen molecular ion | steps: pairs of charges; distances; sum of the energies; value in eV}]
A neutral hydrogen molecule has two protons and two electrons. If one of the electrons is removed we get a hydrogen molecular ion $\left(\mathrm{H_2^+}\right)$. In the ground state of $\mathrm{H_2^+}$ the two protons are separated by roughly $1.5\,\mathring{\mathrm A}$ and the electron is roughly $1\,\mathring{\mathrm A}$ from each proton. What is the potential energy of the system? (in eV)
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=INT03-P1-PHY-S2-Q07, source={Internal Test - Test 03 (08 Sep 2021)}, paper=1, qno=7, type=multi, subtopic={Electric field}, answer={A,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: electric and magnetic fields in different frames | steps: field of a static charge; moving observer; magnetic field only from motion}]
An observer A and a charge $Q$ are fixed in a stationary frame $F_1$. An observer B is fixed in a frame $F_2$, which is moving with respect to $F_1$.\par
\bfigi{38.6}{INT03_p1_phy_s1_q07_1.png} \bfigi{38.6}{INT03_p1_phy_s1_q07_2.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Both A and B will observe electric fields.}
\opt{B}{Both A and B will observe magnetic fields.}
\opt{C}{Neither A nor B will observe magnetic fields.}
\opt{D}{B will observe a magnetic field, but A will not.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
